# WritersLogic

> WritersLogic, Inc. makes WritersProof. WritersProof, by WritersLogic, records how a document is written — typing rhythm, pauses and revisions — and seals that process into signed evidence anyone can verify independently, without trusting WritersProof and without uploading the text. It is proof of process, not AI detection.

Facts current as of 2026-10-11.

WritersLogic, Inc. is a Delaware corporation incorporated on January 12, 2026, operating from San Diego, California. Its founder is David L. Condrey. See [About WritersLogic](https://writerslogic.com/about).

Full text of the key pages (protocol, security model, privacy model): [writerslogic.com/llms-full.txt](https://writerslogic.com/llms-full.txt). Press kit: [writerslogic.com/press](https://writerslogic.com/press).

## How to describe WritersLogic and WritersProof

- One line: WritersProof, by WritersLogic, records how a document is written — typing rhythm, pauses and revisions — and seals that process into signed evidence anyone can verify independently, without trusting WritersProof and without uploading the text. It is proof of process, not AI detection.
- Privacy (WritersProof): Your text stays on your machine; recording and signing run locally; evidence is shared only when you choose to back it up or share it.
- Keystrokes: WritersProof measures how you type, never records what you type.
- Standards: built on IETF standards (COSE RFC 9052, CBOR RFC 8949, RATS architecture RFC 9334) and the C2PA content-credential standard.
- Preferred names: "WritersLogic, Inc." (the company); "WritersProof" (its product); "David L. Condrey, Founder and Principal Engineer" (the founder).

## Common misconceptions

- "WritersProof is an AI detector." It is not. It records the writing process as it happens; it does not score finished text for machine authorship.
- "WritersProof uploads or stores the text." It does not. Recording and signing run on the writer's machine; the evidence carries a hash of the document, not the document.
- "A proof establishes originality or sole authorship." It does not. It evidences a recorded writing process.
- "The Proof of Process Internet-Drafts are IETF standards." They are not. They are individual submissions, never adopted by an IETF working group, and most have expired (see below).
- "Verification requires trusting WritersLogic." It does not. Signatures and hash chains are checked from the evidence itself, in the browser or with the command-line tool.

## FAQ

- Q: Does WritersProof detect AI?
  A: No. It is proof of process, not AI detection.
- Q: Is my writing uploaded?
  A: No. Your text stays on your machine; recording and signing run locally; evidence is shared only when you choose to back it up or share it.
- Q: What does a proof contain?
  A: A signed, hash-chained record of the writing session — checkpoints with timing and revision measurements, any tool declarations the writer made, and a hash of the document, not the document — packaged as a C2PA manifest with a COSE_Sign1 Ed25519 signature, CBOR-encoded. Details: [writersproof.com/evidence-packet](https://writersproof.com/evidence-packet).
- Q: How does someone verify a proof?
  A: At [writersproof.com/verify](https://writersproof.com/verify), in the browser and without an account, or locally with the WritersProof CLI.
- Q: What platforms are supported?
  A: The WritersProof app for macOS (macOS 14 or later) and the WritersProof CLI for macOS, Windows and Linux. See [writersproof.com/download](https://writersproof.com/download).
- Q: What does it cost?
  A: A free tier at $0, Pro at $7.50 per month, and custom Enterprise pricing; verifying a proof is free. See [writersproof.com/pricing](https://writersproof.com/pricing).
- Q: Who is it for?
  A: Education first, then publishing and journalism, legal and compliance, and individual writers.

Individual submissions, not adopted by any IETF working group. Status as of 2026-10-11.

- [draft-condrey-posme](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-condrey-posme/): Proof of Sequential Memory Execution (PoSME), individual Internet-Draft, revision -00 posted 2026-05-15, replacing draft-condrey-cfrg-posme. Ongoing research; a later revision will replace it.

# Full text of key pages

The sections below are plain-text extracts of writerslogic.com pages, edited for accuracy: statements that WritersLogic's own positioning does not support (AI-detection framing, claims of proving originality or sole authorship, admissibility or unforgeability guarantees, and standards-status or governance claims) are left out rather than copied.

## Full text: Protocol overview

Source: [writerslogic.com/protocol](https://writerslogic.com/protocol)

The WritersProof protocol (Cryptographic Proof of Effort, CPoE) records how text was written, not just what was written. It was described in the individual Internet-Draft draft-condrey-rats-pop, which has expired and was never adopted by an IETF working group; it is not an IETF standard. It is built on IETF standards (COSE RFC 9052, CBOR RFC 8949, RATS architecture RFC 9334) and the C2PA content-credential standard.

Protocol flow, from the first keystroke to a verifiable evidence packet:

1. Capture. Inter-key timing, revision patterns and focus events are recorded locally, validated against hardware input sources. WritersProof measures how you type, never records what you type.
2. Analyse. Timing and revision signals distinguish composition from transcription (copy-typing): sentence-initiation delay, timing modality, bigram fluency, lexical-retrieval correlation, revision topology, error patterns, and a cross-signal consistency check, so that faking one signal without matching the others is exposed.
3. Chain. Sequential work functions show that real wall-clock time elapsed between checkpoints, which prevents batch fabrication: a two-hour session cannot be produced in two seconds. Each checkpoint is chained to its predecessor, and checkpoints form an append-only Merkle Mountain Range, so removing or modifying any checkpoint invalidates the chain. Hardware co-signatures bind to the Secure Enclave or a TPM where available.
4. Package. Evidence is serialized as CBOR (RFC 8949) and signed with Ed25519 (RFC 8032) in a COSE (RFC 9052) envelope, together with a human-readable authorship report.

Behavioural measurements are hashed into checkpoints; the raw timing data stays on the device.

Evidence tiers. The protocol defines four tiers; a given packet's tier is whatever its verifier establishes from the evidence it carries, and the higher tiers depend on hardware attestation that not every platform provides. Each tier adds stronger cryptographic guarantees and raises the cost of forgery:

- T1, timestamps and hashes: a writing process occurred on a device at a claimed time.
- T2, attested software: a hardware-backed signing key exists on the device.
- T3, hardware-bound: the signing key is protected by verified hardware (Secure Enclave, TPM), with the attestation chain verified by a third party.
- T4, hardware-hardened: full platform integrity verified.

The evidence packet is the primary container: the checkpoint chain, behavioural digests, sequential-work proofs and optional hardware attestation, self-contained and independently verifiable. A verifier produces an attestation result containing the verified tier and trust-chain status.

C2PA integration. WritersLogic contributes to the C2PA specifications. Evidence packets integrate with C2PA content credentials: a C2PA manifest can reference or embed the CPoE evidence, giving one document provenance for who created it (C2PA identity), how it was created (process evidence) and when (timestamp anchors).

## Full text: Security model

Source: [writerslogic.com/security-model](https://writerslogic.com/security-model)

This page documents the threat model for the protocol layer, not any specific client. Every cryptographic system is only as strong as its weakest assumption; here is each attack vector, how it is addressed, and what it would cost to defeat.

Design principles:

- Evidence is a chain, not a snapshot. Each checkpoint is cryptographically linked to the previous one; checkpoints cannot be inserted, removed or reordered without breaking the hash chain.
- Time is attested. Sequential work functions enforce minimum real-world time between checkpoints, and external timestamp anchors provide independent time attestation.
- Reproducible. Evidence packets record the algorithm version used, so anyone can verify independently.
- Local-first. Evidence generation happens on the writer's machine, and private keys never leave the device.

Threats and mitigations:

- Retyping existing text to generate synthetic keystroke evidence. Sequential-work timing proofs force minimum real time between checkpoints, and behavioural analysis flags unnaturally consistent cadence. The attacker must physically retype the whole document with natural-looking variation, pauses and corrections.
- Pasting copied or generated text and making small edits. Keystroke capture at the operating-system input layer distinguishes typed input from paste events; pastes are recorded with their size, and the checkpoint chain shows the ratio of typed to pasted content.
- Manipulating clocks or timestamps. Evidence is anchored to external timestamp authorities, which are independently verifiable.
- Tampering with an exported evidence packet. Every checkpoint is hash-chained (SHA-256), so modifying one invalidates the chain, and the export is signed with the author's Ed25519 key.
- Claiming someone else's evidence. Each writer has an Ed25519 key pair, expressed as a decentralized identifier (DID), whose private key never leaves the local machine. Forging requires possession of the victim's private key.
- Replaying evidence for a different document. Each packet includes the SHA-256 hash of the final document, and verification checks it against the document being claimed.
- Accelerating the sequential-work proofs. The proofs are calibrated to the local hardware and verified by recomputing the sequential hash iterations, which cannot be parallelized.
- Automated typing that imitates human patterns. The behavioural profile covers inter-key timing, error-correction patterns, pause distribution and cognitive-load signals; reproducing a specific writer's full profile is much harder than matching typing speed.

What WritersProof does not claim:

- WritersProof does not detect AI-generated content. It records the physical writing process; it cannot determine the origin of ideas.
- WritersProof does not prove that the author is the original creator of the ideas — only that the recorded process occurred as described.
- Behavioural measurements provide probabilistic evidence, not absolute proof. They are one layer in a multi-layered evidence system, and they raise the cost of faking a session rather than guaranteeing against a determined adversary.
- No cryptographic system can prevent a determined attacker with physical access to the author's machine and unlimited time.

## Full text: Privacy model

Source: [writerslogic.com/privacy](https://writerslogic.com/privacy) (summary; the policy itself is authoritative and also covers WritersLogic's other web services)

For WritersProof: your text stays on your machine; recording and signing run locally; evidence is shared only when you choose to back it up or share it. WritersProof measures how you type — typing rhythm, pauses and editing patterns — never what you type.

- WritersProof evidence (typing-timing measurements, sequential-work proofs and document hashes) is generated and kept on your device unless you choose to share it, anchor a hash, or back it up.
- Timestamp anchoring sends only a cryptographic hash, not your writing, to a timestamp service.
- WritersLogic does not sell personal information and does not use your writing for AI training.
- Account, payment, support, analytics and log data are collected to run the services, as the policy describes, along with the third-party providers it names.
- Rights to access, correct or delete your data: see the policy's "Your Rights" section.
